About me

I’ve always been curious about how people make decisions and what shapes their choices. Psychology gave me a way to actually answer it. Now, whenever I use a product, I ask what the person on the other side is thinking, feeling and trying to get done, and where the design gets in their way.

I believe research is only worth doing if it changes something people actually use. A finding that stays in a document helps no one, but one that makes a product clearer, faster or less frustrating does. That’s the standard I hold my own work to.

B2B SaaS · Independent case study

HexoHub

From stalled work to accountable follow-up

A B2B project management concept for coordinators who run team check-ins. It brings overdue and blocked tasks into one view before the meeting and lets coordinators verify AI-suggested follow-ups before adding them to the project.

My roleSolo UX research, interaction design and prototyping
MethodsCompetitive analysis of Trello and Asana, public user review analysis and an exploratory survey
OutcomeA clickable Figma prototype covering task triage, AI recap review and task approval
StatusPrototype complete for a guided walkthrough. Usability testing pending.

Explore the HexoHub prototype in Figma

Context and product opportunity

Before a check-in, a coordinator needs to decide which tasks to discuss and whose help is needed. After the meeting, they need to turn commitments into work the team can track. If a blocker is missed or a follow-up has no clear owner, dependent work can slip and the team may have to revisit the same issue at the next meeting.

I focused on two decisions within that workflow: what needs attention before the meeting, and what should become a task after it.

Discovery and synthesis

I compared how Trello and Asana organize shared work, focusing on task views, filters, and the visibility of overdue or blocked tasks. I also reviewed public user feedback and ran an exploratory survey to understand how people find work that needs attention.

The reviews surfaced difficulty keeping an overview as projects grew. One survey response complicated that picture. An experienced Asana user reported that finding overdue or blocked tasks was easy even on a large project, because their existing workflow worked for them.

That changed the scope. I had assumed board size was the main source of friction. I narrowed the design question to coordinators who already check overdue and blocked work separately: can a combined view help them prepare for a check-in without overlooking or double-counting tasks?

Design decisions

1. Make the project list the main working view

My first iteration put summary metrics above the task list. Design critique and the Asana walkthrough pointed to a better fit for the coordinator’s immediate job: a list with a compact toolbar and enough room to scan task details. I moved project metrics to Overview and made the List the main view for triage.

Within the list, Needs attention brings overdue and blocked work together. A task that meets both conditions appears once and carries both flags. Separate filters still support a more targeted review. The tradeoff is an extra view to maintain, so its value depends on whether it improves check-in preparation.

2. Make AI suggestions reviewable before they become assignments

Automatic task creation would save a step, but it could also turn a misread commitment into assigned work. I chose an explicit review step. HexoHub labels the recap as an AI-generated draft, puts the source notes beside the suggestions, and leaves missing ownership or dates visible. The coordinator decides what enters the project.

The prototype deliberately suggests “Book the interview room” when the source note says the team needs a pilot room. That gives a usability session a concrete failure case: can someone notice the mismatch and correct it before approving a follow-up?

3. Make the result of approval easy to verify

Approval changes the shared project, so the coordinator needs clear feedback about what happened. I added a confirmation and showed the resulting task in context, with its assignee, due date and a link back to the recap. The walkthrough demonstrates a selective handoff: the coordinator reviews multiple suggestions and adds the consent checklist task.

Outcome and validation

The prototype demonstrates the workflow from finding stalled work to verifying an approved follow-up. It uses demo data and scripted interactions. Whether it reduces preparation time, missed tasks or incorrect assignments remains unmeasured.

What I’d testWhat I’d measureHow I’d use the result
Combined view vs. separate filters using equivalent task setsTime to identify work that needs attention, tasks missed, tasks incorrectly flaggedIf coordinators perform similarly with separate filters, I’d reconsider whether the combined view earns a permanent place in the project list.
AI recap review with a deliberate error and no hint about where it isWhether participants check the source, catch the mismatch and correctly identify the task added after approvalIf participants miss the error, I’d revise how the source is presented and test whether the change helps them catch it.

Reflection

The most useful feedback came from someone whose existing workflow already worked. It pushed me to design for a specific coordination problem and set a clearer standard for the next iteration: a combined view has to help people find the right work, and AI assistance has to make suggested commitments easy to verify before the team acts on them.

From sign-up to first API call

A self-guided walkthrough of Sarvam’s developer onboarding, from landing on the site to a first API call.

My roleSolo researcher, playing a first-time user
MethodTimed walkthrough with notes at each step, a friction log and a check of the official docs afterwards
ResultBlocked at the first call by a “No credits available” error after about 27–30 minutes (approximate)
StatusComplete. One person, one session, so this is not research with participants.

An independent exercise. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by Sarvam.

Context

Sarvam builds AI models and APIs for Indian languages. The first API call is the moment a developer decides whether to keep going, which makes it a good place to look for friction. I took the view of someone with a psychology background and little coding experience, such as a PM or founder trying the API for the first time. I chose “Researcher” when asked which role suits me, on a pay-as-you-go account with no credits added, using Windows PowerShell.

The journey

PhaseRoughly whenWhat happened
Landing to Quickstartfirst ~3 minScanned the homepage, clicked “Get started”, reached the Quickstart. Felt right so far.
Account creation~3–6 minSigned up with an emailed verification code. Smooth.
Setup questions~6–10 minChose a role (Researcher), then LLMs vs voice (LLMs).
API key page~11 minThe page asked me to download the SDK. I didn’t know how or where.
Back to the Quickstart~13 minWent back to understand the next step and found the environment variable step.
Terminal setup~20–30 minPasted the key into PowerShell and set it again. Python wasn’t found on my computer, so I switched to curl.exe, which comes with Windows.
First callendThe translation call returned “No credits available.” with the code insufficient_quota_error.

What worked well

Landing to the Quickstart took one click and about three minutes. Account creation with an emailed code was quick and clear, and the role and product questions were easy to answer. The error itself was well structured: a readable message, a specific code and a request ID I could quote to support.

Friction log

StepWhat I expectedWhat happenedSeverity
API key pageA way to continue without knowing what an SDK isThe page asked me to download the SDK without saying how or where, so I went back to the QuickstartMedium
Terminal setupTo paste the example and run itIt wasn’t clear where to paste it or which window to use, and Python wasn’t installed. Setup took roughly 15 minutes.Medium
First callA working response“No credits available.”, with no next step in the messageHigh

Findings and recommendations

1. The key page assumes you know what an SDK is

The next instruction after creating a key was to download the SDK, with no explanation of how. A new developer may leave the page to find out. Recommendation: add one line saying how to get the SDK, or offer a first call that needs no install.

2. The Quickstart assumes terminal experience

It lists Python or Node.js as prerequisites but doesn’t explain how to get them, or where to type and run the example. For someone who has never used a terminal, this is where the journey slows most. Recommendation: add a short “before you start” box covering what a terminal is, what to install and which window to use.

3. The first call ended with “No credits available”, and the error doesn’t say what to do next

The message was clear about what happened but not what to do. Sarvam’s Errors and Troubleshooting page, which I checked afterwards, covers this exact error and says to add credits in Settings, then Billing. That is a separate page, and the error doesn’t point to it. I don’t know why my account had no credits, since Sarvam’s docs say new accounts receive ₹100 in free credits. Recommendation: put the next step in the message itself, and show the credit balance before the first call in the Quickstart.

A psychology link

The key page and Quickstart seem written by people who know the setup well. That is the curse of knowledge: once you know something, it’s hard to remember what it was like not to. Small gaps that feel obvious to the writer add up to real effort for a newcomer.

What I’d do next

Watch 3–5 developers with different experience levels attempt the same task and compare where they hesitate. One person can show that a gap exists, but not how common it is.
